The first two schemas track the same determination cycle at different resolutions. The event-centred schema presents the cycle dynamically, by distinguishing the recurrent operations—model design, experiment design, determination and validation—through which inquiry is organised, redirected and assessed, without assigning those operations to specific devices. The device-centred schema complements this projection by locating the mediating devices that cooperate within the same practice—object model, target system, measuring instrument and measuring model—while leaving their temporal unfolding comparatively backgrounded. The crossing of causal salience identified in Section 3 thus becomes visible as a redistribution of work across both events and devices, without collapsing model systems and measuring systems into a single undifferentiated structure. Yet each of these devices can in turn be treated as the distinctive component of a wider system in which it is embedded. A third schema is therefore needed at the system scale, where devices and events are considered together as parts of a stabilised arrangement through which a pattern is deployed, maintained and revised across contexts. The system-centred schema arranges this stabilised arrangement across symbolic and empirical ambits, while replacing the pattern/node distinction with a contrast between organisation and implementation (Figure 3).

  

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 3. System-centred schema displaying the stabilised circuit through which an epistemic framework, an operational field, an experimental setup and an experiment design coordinate deployment, coupling, records and codification.

  

The epistemic framework occupies the symbolic side of system organisation. It includes the models, standards, classifications, admissibility criteria, performance thresholds, reporting categories and inferential routines through which a stabilised pattern can guide further practice. Its role is wider than that of an object model, since it does not merely organise a target system for one modelling task; it fixes the symbolic environment in which the pattern becomes portable, assessable and usable across a range of cases. In that sense, it resembles the kind of classificatory and standardising infrastructure through which scientific and technical objects become stable enough to circulate across communities, institutions and domains of application (Bowker & Star, 1999; Timmermans & Epstein, 2010).

The operational field occupies the empirical side of system organisation. It is the field in which the stabilised pattern is expected to operate: a clinical environment, a technological infrastructure, a manufacturing process, an ecological site, a regulatory domain or an extended field of use. At this level, the empirical counterpart of the model is no longer a target system isolated for focused determination, but a broader environment in which the pattern is embedded among routines, disturbances, users, artefacts and institutional constraints. Deployment names the movement from epistemic framework to operational field: the framework projects a stabilised pattern into a domain of use by specifying which features are relevant, which deviations count as significant, which ranges remain admissible and which actions can be guided by the resulting outcomes.

The lower half of the schema locates system implementation. The experimental setup occupies the empirical side: it comprises the devices, instruments, material supports, sampling arrangements, calibration infrastructures, computational pipelines, maintenance routines and environmental controls through which the operational field is coupled to a determination pathway. The term experiment should be read broadly, by including laboratory experiment, field measurement, clinical validation, technical testing, quality-control procedures and post-deployment surveillance. Stabilisation often occurs after the initial pattern has left the narrow laboratory setting and entered larger infrastructures of use. In such contexts, reliability depends less on a single successful measurement than on the maintained coordination between framework, field, setup and design. Furthermore, coupling is here the empirical mediation through which a selected part of the operational field is made accessible to the setup. This relation may take the form of intervention, sampling, monitoring, sensing, surveillance or routine use. Its point is to secure a reproducible contact between the deployed pattern and the field in which it must continue to hold under variation.

Operational design occupies the symbolic side of system implementation. The term refer the codified design of the determination regime: protocols, calibration rules, reference procedures, sampling schemes, validation criteria, admissible tolerances, documentation formats and revision rules. Records name the movement from experimental setup to experiment design. Signals, traces, logs, readings, failures, quality-control results and performance profiles are gathered and formatted so that they can be assessed within the rules governing the determination regime. The epistemic significance of records depends on their position within this design: the same trace may count as ordinary variability, drift, malfunction, threshold-crossing or evidence for redesign depending on the codified role it receives.

Codification closes the circuit by relating experiment design back to the epistemic framework. Recurrent records become epistemically consequential only when they are converted into revised constraints, updated standards, altered admissibility conditions, new reporting categories or modified scope claims. This is the point at which stabilisation becomes cumulative. The system does not merely repeat a successful determination pathway; it incorporates the history of its own performance into the framework that will govern later deployments. In metrological and standardising practices, such portability is often achieved through the circulation of locally produced particulars—reference materials, calibration chains, procedural conventions and comparison records—that acquire general force by being repeatedly codified across sites (O’Connell, 1993).

In presence of a deviation detected, this schema allows to distinguish where the stabilised pattern has lost portability. A deviation may arise because the epistemic framework was deployed beyond its legitimate scope, because the operational field introduced conditions insufficiently represented in the framework, because coupling between field and setup became unstable, because records were generated or formatted under unsuitable conditions, or because codification failed to transform recurrent deviations into revised constraints.
